full_query: A 46-year-old man presents with his wife to his primary care provider for depression and strange movements. His wife reports that her husband has not been himself for the last 2 months. Whereas he was previously outgoing and “the life of the party,” the patient is now irritable and withdrawn. He is a partner at an accounting firm, but his colleagues are threatening to fire him if he continues to perform poorly at work. The patient cannot explain the recent changes to his mood and tearfully admits he fears there is something seriously wrong with him. His wife says that he is getting worse. The patient’s medical history is significant for hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril. His family history is unknown as he was adopted. The patient met his mother once and never knew his father but was told he died in his 50s. He drinks a few glasses of wine per week and has never smoked. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 141/87 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, the patient has a flat affect with a facial grimace and sudden jerky movements of his upper extremities. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on further workup? (A) Alpha-synuclein aggregates on brain biopsy (B) Dorsal striatum atrophy on head CT (C) Frontotemporal atrophy on head CT (D) Neurofibrillary tangles on brain biopsy (E) Positive 14-3-3 CSF assay

sentences: To approach the query methodically, let's start by analyzing the patient's presentation and history
Age: 46-year-old male
Symptoms: Depression, strange movements, irritability, withdrawal from social interactions, poor work performance
Physical exam: Flat affect, facial grimace, sudden jerky movements of upper extremities
Significant past medical history: Hypertension, managed with lisinopril
Family history: Adopted, minimal information, but noted his father died in his 50s
Temperature: 98.6°F (37°C)
Blood pressure: 141/87 mmHg
Pulse: 81/min
Respirations: 12/min

The combination of psychiatric symptoms (depression, irritability) and neurological signs (jerky movements, flat affect, facial grimace) in a middle-aged individual, along with a family history of early death in the father, strongly suggests a neurodegenerative disorder
Huntington's disease (HD): Progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor dysfunction (chorea), psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive decline
The patient's symptoms and age are consistent with HD
Parkinson's disease (PD): Characterized by bradykinesia, rigidity, tremors, and sometimes psychiatric symptoms
However, the patient's jerky movements (chorea) are not typical for PD
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD): Behavioral changes and executive dysfunction are prominent, but motor symptoms as described are less characteristic
Alzheimer's disease (AD): Primarily affects memory and cognitive functions, not typically associated with chorea
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD): Rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and positive 14-3-3 CSF assay
Considering the symptoms and the family history, Huntington's disease is the most likely diagnosis
Huntington's disease typically shows
Dorsal striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) atrophy on head CT or MRI
This atrophy is a hallmark of the disease and can be detected with imaging studies
(A) Alpha-synuclein aggregates on brain biopsy: Seen in Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy
Not consistent with the patient's presentation
(B) Dorsal striatum atrophy on head CT: Consistent with Huntington's disease
(C) Frontotemporal atrophy on head CT: Seen in frontotemporal dementia
Less likely given the motor symptoms
(D) Neurofibrillary tangles on brain biopsy: Characteristic of Alzheimer's disease
Not consistent with the patient's motor symptoms
(E) Positive 14-3-3 CSF assay: Indicative of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
This disease progresses rapidly and is less consistent with the gradual symptom onset described
After thorough consideration, the most likely finding on further workup for this patient is
(B) Dorsal striatum atrophy on head CT
